Ship trajectory¶

Summary¶

ShipTrajectory builds a ship’s route from a start point, an end point, a start time, and a speed. The route stays on water and is time-stamped: it is a list of (timestamp, latitude, longitude) samples. The moving-target detector (MovingTargetDetection) reads these samples to place the target at each time step.

The route is planned on a navigation mesh – a graph of points on the sea. The points come from an ocean-polygon shapefile (Constants.earth_coastline_path; Natural Earth ne_10m_ocean.shp by default, though any water-polygon layer works – see the assumptions below). Points that fall on water become graph nodes, and two nodes are linked when the straight line between them stays on water. The shortest path across this graph is the route (found with networkx). A start or end point on land is moved to the nearest water. The finished route is simplified, sampled at a fixed time step, and saved to disk, so an unchanged run loads it back instead of planning it again.

Detailed Module Description¶

Endpoint conditioning¶

Each endpoint must sit on water. If an endpoint is on land, it is moved to the nearest water and pushed a little further out by the water_buffer margin (default 22.2 km, or 12 nautical miles – the territorial-sea limit). The shoreline direction is found in geographic coordinates, converted to local east/north metres with WGS-84 radii of curvature, normalised there, and converted back to latitude and longitude after applying the metre-valued buffer.

Navigation mesh and graph¶

A box is drawn around the two endpoints and filled with a grid of points, spaced grid_resolution_km apart. The east-west spacing grows with latitude (fn.delta_lon_from_distance) so the grid stays roughly even in kilometres. Only points on water are kept as nodes. Two nodes are joined by an edge when they are closer than mesh_connection_radius and the straight line between them stays on water; the edge length is the great-circle (haversine) distance. A cKDTree makes the search for nearby points fast.

Shortest path and component bridging¶

The route is the shortest path from start to end through the graph (networkx.shortest_path, using the edge lengths as weights). Sometimes the start and end fall in two separate pieces of the graph – for example, split by a narrow strait the grid stepped over. When that happens, _bridge_components looks for short, water-only links between the two pieces (using a Delaunay triangulation, and adding midpoints in tight passages if needed) until they join up.

Path simplification and sampling¶

simplify_path drops waypoints that are not needed: if skipping a waypoint still keeps the path on water, it is removed, leaving only the real corners. The simplified route is then sampled in time. generate_trajectory_equal_time splits the total travel time across the legs by their length and places a sample every interval_minutes, moving in a straight line in (lat, lon) along each leg. generate_trajectory_equal_dist instead places a sample every fixed number of metres. The total travel time comes from the route length and the ship speed: end_time = start_time + route_distance / ship_speed.

Distance and bearing¶

Leg lengths use the haversine great-circle distance on a sphere of radius Constants.RADIUS_EARTH_EQUAT,

(74)¶\[a = \sin^2\! \left(\frac{\Delta\phi}{2}\right) + \cos \left( \phi_1 \right)\,\cos\left( \phi_2 \right)\,\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\Delta\lambda}{2}\right), \qquad d = 2R\,\arcsin\!\sqrt{a},\]

where \(\phi\) is latitude and \(\lambda\) is longitude. The starting heading from one point to the next is

(75)¶\[\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left( \sin(\Delta\lambda)\cos\phi_2,\; \cos\phi_1\sin\phi_2-\sin\phi_1\cos\phi_2\cos(\Delta\lambda) \right),\]

wrapped to the range [0, 360) degrees.

Caching¶

create_trajectory_files saves the route as a shapefile plus a small JSON file with its settings (positions, speed, start time, interval, mesh parameters). Next time, _cache_matches_inputs reuses the saved route only if the start/end points, start time, speed, interval, fast-method flag, grid resolution, connection radius, water buffer and bounding-box margin all match. Missing fields in an older cache make it stale.

Public interface¶

class object_definitions.ShipTrajectory_def.ShipTrajectory(ship_id, ship_speed_knot, start_position, start_time, end_position, interval_minutes=10, grid_resolution_km=50, delta_boudingBox_km=500, fast_path_gen_method=True, mesh_connection_radius_km=2000, water_buffer_km=22.2, trajectory_type=None, save_graph=False)[source]¶

Time-stamped, land-avoiding maritime route for a single ship.

Plans a route from start_position to end_position over a navigation mesh built from the Natural Earth ocean polygons, time-samples it at a fixed interval, and writes a trajectory shapefile plus metadata JSON (cached between runs).

Parameters:

  • ship_id (str) – Unique identifier; used for the shapefile / cache filenames.

  • ship_speed_knot (float) – Cruise speed [knots]; stored internally as m/s.

  • start_position (tuple) – Start point (latitude, longitude); snapped to water if on land.

  • start_time (datetime) – Journey start (UTC).

  • end_position (tuple) – End point (latitude, longitude); snapped to water if on land.

  • interval_minutes (int, optional) – Time-sampling interval [min] for the trajectory (default 10).

  • grid_resolution_km (float, optional) – Navigation-mesh grid spacing [km] (default 50); dominates planning cost.

  • delta_boudingBox_km (float, optional) – Margin [km] added around the endpoints’ bounding box (default 500).

  • fast_path_gen_method (bool, optional) – Use the simplified (faster, coarser) path generator (default True).

  • mesh_connection_radius_km (float, optional) – Maximum edge length [km] when connecting mesh nodes (default 2000).

  • water_buffer_km (float, optional) – Safety margin from shore [km] (default 22.2 = 12 nautical miles).

  • trajectory_type (list, optional) – Extra shapefile types to also write (“points”, “line”, “waypoints”).

  • save_graph (bool, optional) – Persist the navigation graph to disk for inspection (default False).

Module Assumptions and Limitations¶

  • Round-Earth distances. Distances assume a perfect sphere, not the slightly flattened real Earth. The error is well under 1% – much smaller than the grid spacing – so it does not matter here.

  • Straight lines between waypoints. Between two waypoints the ship moves in a straight line in latitude/longitude, not along a true great circle. This is fine for short legs and rougher for very long ones.

  • One fixed speed. The ship travels at a single cruise speed. There is no speeding up, slowing down, current, or weather.

  • Which shapefile you can use. The water data is not tied to Natural Earth. Any vector file that geopandas.read_file() can open works (.shp, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, …), as long as it (1) stores the water as polygons (the code treats inside a polygon as water), and (2) uses longitude/latitude in degrees (EPSG:4326), since distances are measured straight from those coordinates. Natural Earth ne_10m_ocean.shp is the default; point Constants.earth_coastline_path at another file to change it. A land or coastline-line file would flip the water test and break the routing.

  • Route detail depends on the grid. How well the route avoids land depends on grid_resolution_km and mesh_connection_radius_km. fast_path_gen_method gives a faster run with a rougher route. Both endpoints must be on open water that can be reached (an endpoint on land is moved to a 12 nm buffer).

  • Shore buffer is locally planar. The metre/degree conversion uses local WGS-84 curvature, but the nearest polygon boundary and its direction are still found in EPSG:4326 planar coordinates. This is adequate for a local buffer, not a geodesic coastal-distance guarantee.

  • Position lookup is approximate. get_position_at_time returns the nearest stored sample, not an exact interpolated position.

  • Shapefiles are only for viewing. They are written in EPSG:4326 for use in GIS tools; the simulation itself uses trajectory_points and timestamps directly.

Validation and Tests¶

Building the full object needs the large (>100 MB) ocean shapefile, so tests/test_ship_trajectory.py skips __init__ (with object.__new__) and tests the helper functions on their own:

Test group

What it checks

TestHaversineDistance

Zero distance for identical points; one degree of latitude ~ 111 km; Oslo->Trondheim ~ 392 km; antipodal points ~ \(\pi R\); symmetry.

TestHaversineVectorized

The vectorized form returns one distance per pair and matches the scalar haversine; the clip(a, 0, 1) guard returns 0 (not NaN) for coincident points.

TestCalculateBearing

Due north / east / south / west give 0 / 90 / 180 / 270 deg; results always lie in [0, 360).

TestSafeWaterPoint

A 22.2 km buffer is converted from metres to angular coordinates and lands approximately 22.2 km inside a simple water polygon.

TestTrajectoryCacheLoading

Matching metadata reloads the cache (no re-plan); changed speed or mesh resolution marks it stale and forces a re-plan.

User Guide¶

The route inputs come from the moving-target configuration file. The mesh-resolution settings are currently set in code, where the trajectory is built in main_simulation_movingTarget.py (they are not in the INI file yet).

Table 24: Route inputs (INI)¶

INI key

Constructor argument

[MOVING TARGET].speed

ship_speed_knot (knots).

[MOVING TARGET].start_pos

start_position as [latitude, longitude].

[MOVING TARGET].end_pos

end_position as [latitude, longitude].

[SIMULATION SETTINGS].starttime

start_time (UTC epoch).

 
from datetime import datetime, UTC
from object_definitions.ShipTrajectory_def import ShipTrajectory

ship = ShipTrajectory(
    ship_id="DarkShip_001",
    ship_speed_knot=15.0,
    start_position=(54.199416, 7.892937),   # (lat, lon) -- Helgoland
    start_time=datetime(2026, 5, 31, 12, 0, 0, tzinfo=UTC),
    end_position=(69.345572, 33.646450),    # (lat, lon) -- Murmansk
    interval_minutes=10,
    grid_resolution_km=150,
    fast_path_gen_method=False,
)

pos = ship.get_position_at_time(datetime(2026, 5, 31, 18, 0, 0, tzinfo=UTC))

References¶

  • Sinnott, R. W., “Virtues of the Haversine”, Sky and Telescope 68(2), 1984.

  • Douglas, D. & Peucker, T., “Algorithms for the reduction of the number of points required to represent a digitized line or its caricature”, Cartographica 10(2), 1973.

  • Hagberg, A., Schult, D. & Swart, P., “Exploring network structure, dynamics, and function using NetworkX”, Proc. 7th Python in Science Conf. (SciPy), 2008.
